shenanigans.summary: Elevated forensic risk — 3 high and 4 medium red flag(s). Treat reported earnings/cash skeptically and work the checklist.

items: EM1 — Revenue too soon: Is revenue booked before delivery/acceptance or while material contingencies remain? Are receivables (DSO) outgrowing sales?
EM2 — Bogus revenue: Does revenue include items lacking economic substance — related-party sales, barter/round-trip deals, or vendor financing booked as revenue?
EM3 — One-time boosts: Is income inflated by asset-sale or investment gains shown within operations, or by releasing reserves ('cookie-jar' accounting)?
EM4 — Shifting current expenses later: Are normal operating costs being capitalized (software, customer acquisition) or parked on the balance sheet?
EM5 — Hiding expenses/losses: Are real costs (stock comp, restructuring, pension) excluded from the headline 'adjusted' number, or losses kept off-balance-sheet?
EM6 — Shifting current income later: In a strong year, is income deferred (over-reserving, deferring revenue) to smooth future periods?
EM7 — Shifting future expenses earlier: Is a 'big bath' write-off overstating today's charge to relieve future periods?
CF1 — Financing inflows into CFO: Is operating cash flow boosted by selling/securitizing receivables or vendor financing routed through the operating section?
CF2 — Operating outflows out of CFO: Are operating costs reclassified to investing/financing (capitalized outlays, 'boomerang' transactions)?
CF3 — Unsustainable CFO: Is CFO propped up by stretching payables (rising DPO), under-buying inventory, or one-off working-capital releases that cannot repeat?

KM1 — Misleading metrics: Does management lean on a self-defined metric (adjusted EBITDA, 'cash earnings', bookings, organic growth) whose definition shifts or diverges from GAAP? (Valeant touted 'cash earnings'; Whirlpool ran 'restructuring' charges in 23 of 27 years before the SEC objected in Oct 2016.)

KM2 — Hidden balance-sheet decay: Are deteriorating ratios masked — factoring receivables to flatter DSO, dodging impairment, or excluding debt-like obligations (leases, pensions, factoring) from leverage?
AA1 — Is acquired revenue/cash flow released to flatter pro-forma trends, or are pre-close write-downs used to build future cookie jars?
AA2 — Is goodwill ballooning while ROIC on acquired capital falls — a serial acquirer masking organic stagnation?

shenanigans.method: Detectors are conservative trip-wires from Schilit & Perler, 'Financial Shenanigans' (4th ed.), plus Sloan (1996) accruals and Lev & Gu cash-conversion, the Altman Z-Score (1968) and Beneish M-Score (1999). A flag or score means investigate, not guilt.

rndAdjusted.note: R&D capitalized over a 5-year life (Damodaran, Ch.9). R&D is expensed under GAAP, which understates EBIT and invested capital for research-intensive firms; capitalizing it restates true operating profitability and ROIC. Life is a default assumption — lengthen for pharma/long-cycle R&D, shorten for fast-moving software.

leases.note: Debt value of operating leases (PV of future lease commitments at the pre-tax cost of debt) added to conventional debt; operating income grossed up by the imputed lease interest (Damodaran Ch.9, approximate adjustment).

investmentIncome.note: Interest/investment income (after tax) removed from earnings; marketable securities are valued separately and added back at market value rather than mingled with operating cash flows (Damodaran Ch.9). Excludes financial firms.

oneTime.note: Normalized operating income = the firm's own through-the-cycle median operating margin applied to current revenue, so one good or bad year does not anchor the valuation (Damodaran Ch.9). Flagged years and any inferred goodwill impairment mark candidate one-time distortions.

goodwillSbc.note: Stock-based compensation is a real operating expense and is NOT added back (Damodaran Ch.9) — its dilution and margin drag are shown so the cost is not overlooked. A material year-over-year drop in goodwill is treated as a one-time impairment.

tobinsQ.note: Tobin's Q compares what the market pays for the whole firm with the book value of the assets that produce its profits. A Q well above 1 says the market believes the assets earn more than they cost to assemble. A Q below 1 says the market prices the firm under its asset base.

ownerEarnings.assumption: Maintenance capital spending is estimated with Greenwald's method. It takes capital spending for the year and removes the spending needed to support this year's revenue growth, sized at the firm's average ratio of net property, plant and equipment to sales. What is left is the cost of standing still, so spending beyond it counts as growth. Depreciation and amortization is the fallback when the history is too short to measure that ratio, or when a fiscal year is missing from it. Where upkeep comes out above the year's actual capital spending, the shortfall is shown as under-investment rather than as negative growth spending.
ownerEarnings.note: Owner earnings measure the cash an owner could take out each year without weakening the business. Reported earnings ignore the real cost of upkeep, and free cash flow charges growth spending against today. Owner earnings sit between the two.

dupont.note: 5-step DuPont: ROE = Tax Burden (NI/EBT) × Interest Burden (EBT/EBIT) × EBIT Margin (EBIT/Revenue) × Asset Turnover (Revenue/Avg Total Assets) × Financial Leverage (Avg Total Assets/Avg Equity). EBIT = Operating Income; balance-sheet terms use the average of beginning and ending values. The first three factors multiply to net margin; all five telescope to ROE.

leverageRoe.note: Leverage decomposition: ROE = ROIC + D/E × [ROIC − i(1−t)], where i is the book interest rate (interest expense / book debt) and t the effective tax rate. ROIC is after-tax operating income over book capital (equity + debt). The second term is the leverage gain: borrowed capital earns ROIC but costs i(1−t), and the surplus on every borrowed dollar belongs to equity. A negative spread turns that gain into a drag that grows with D/E.

businessProfile.summary: Rivian Automotive, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, develops, manufactures, and sells category-defining electric vehicles. It operates through two segments, Automotive, and Software and Services. The company offers consumer vehicles, including a two-row, five-passenger pickup truck under the R1T brand; and a three-row, seven-passenger sport utility vehicle under the R1S name. It also provides software and services, such as vehicle electrical architecture and software development, as well as Autonomy+, remarketing, vehicle repair and maintenance services, software subscriptions, vehicle accessories, financing, insurance, and other services. In addition, the company designs, develops, and manufactures the Rivian Adventure Network Direct Current fast chargers; and FleetOS, a proprietary, end-to-end centralized fleet management subscription platform. Further, it offers Rivian Commercial Van platform for Electric Delivery Van with collaboration with Amazon.com, Inc. Rivian Automotive, Inc. was founded in 2009 and is based in Irvine, California.
